segments.line: Day nine. Twenty- five tonnes. You
reach for your toothbrush, and it snaps. You
turn the tap, and the tap comes off.
Water everywhere. Breakfast. Your
spoon folds like paper. Your
phone cracks in your pocket, just because you leaned on it.
Every door in the house has your fingerprints pressed into it.
Here's what nobody tells you about strength. Strength is easy. Control is hard. Your
brain spent fourteen years learning a body that could lift fifty kilos. Now every tiny push is five hundred times too big.
So you start living in slow motion. Fingertips only. Every movement planned.
Day ten. You try to lift Dad's car again, to show him. Your
feet sink into the lawn, right up to your ankles.
Because all that weight still has to go somewhere, down through two small trainers. The
school sends a letter. Please stay at home until further notice.
Then on day eleven, you sneeze, grab the kitchen counter, and
something in your hand goes crack. The
X- ray says fracture. From your own grip.
Remember the rule. Your muscles double. Your bones don't. And
doctors already know what happens when muscles pull harder than bones can take.
During a strong seizure or an electric shock, a person's own muscles can dislocate a shoulder, or even break a bone. That's real. And
now your muscles pull two thousand times harder than they were built to. Then there's
the food. Holding something is free. Lifting it is not.
To lift the Titanic just one metre, you'd burn about the food you eat in two months. And that's if your body wasted nothing.
So you're the strongest person on Earth, and you can't hold a glass of water. Your
little sister runs at you for a hug, and you have to step back.
